work.scope: Fictional library welcome-service concept. No actual service research, staffing agreement, system integration or operational approval is supplied.

pages.title: Connect the visible service to its support.
pages.lead: This proposal explores an imagined library welcome interaction. The blueprint links a visitor action, a visible response and the behind-the-scenes support that might make that response possible.
pages.body: The decision is whether this service concept deserves contextual research and responsible review. The illustrated desk is a visual reference only; it supplies no site dimensions, staffing capacity or evidence about real visitors.

pages.title: Begin with a situation, not a persona claim.
pages.lead: Describe the task a fictional visitor is trying to accomplish and the information they may lack. Avoid presenting a made-up profile as research about an actual population.
pages.body: Example situation: a first-time reader wants to understand where a group discussion might happen. Their familiarity, access needs and preferences remain unknown. A real service proposal would investigate those conditions through appropriate methods.

pages.title: Map the frontstage contact.
pages.lead: Frontstage actions are the visible words, objects and responses a visitor encounters. State what the interaction is intended to clarify rather than promising that it works.
pages.body: A proposed welcome card might explain the purpose of a session and where to ask a question. It should not imply guaranteed availability, accessibility or eligibility. The wording needs review against the real service context before use.

pages.title: Reveal the backstage work.
pages.lead: A simple visible response can depend on preparation that visitors do not see. Put those backstage activities on the same page so the proposal does not hide its implementation burden.
pages.body: A welcome card could require a current session description, an agreed point of contact and a way to update the copy. These are proposed activities; no role or organisation has accepted them through this document.

pages.title: Identify the supporting systems.
pages.lead: Distinguish a service idea from the information and coordination systems it would need. The blueprint should make gaps visible rather than imply that a real technical integration already exists.
pages.body: A current information source, a version record and a route for questions might support the welcome interaction. Do not invent a booking system, identity check or confirmed database connection to make the diagram appear complete.

pages.title: Mark the points of uncertainty.
pages.lead: A breakpoint is a place where the proposed flow could fail to answer the visitor’s question or depend on missing support. Name the uncertainty before selecting a solution.
pages.body: For example, an outdated card could direct a visitor to a session that is not confirmed. The issue might concern information ownership rather than the visual design of the card. These are hypothetical failure modes, not observed incidents.

pages.title: Compare a lighter alternative.
pages.lead: Test the concept against an option with fewer dependencies. An alternative is useful when it pursues the same visitor intention rather than simply offering a different-looking desk.
pages.body: Compare a maintained welcome card with a clearly identified route for asking a question. The latter may reduce copy maintenance but depend more on an available contact. Neither option is confirmed as suitable for a real service.

pages.title: Turn assumptions into research questions.
pages.lead: Translate the most important uncertainties into questions a suitable inquiry could address. Keep proposed research separate from actual findings.
pages.body: Questions might concern what first-time readers need to know, who maintains information and how changes reach the visible touchpoint. An illustration cannot answer any of these questions, and this template contains no participant study.

pages.title: Define the service handoff.
pages.lead: A handoff should identify the current concept version, the unresolved dependencies and the role that would need to accept further work. Passing a file is not the same as transferring responsibility.
pages.body: The proposed package includes a blueprint, copy draft and question list. A real owner would need to confirm which artifacts are useful and which operating conditions apply. Do not label a concept reviewed or approved without that confirmation.

pages.title: Record the concept decision.
pages.lead: Invite a reader to keep, revise or pause the service concept, with a reason tied to its dependencies. A decision record should preserve the uncertainty rather than make the diagram look final.
pages.body: A bounded response might request contextual research before choosing between the card and contact-route options. Keep the distinction between a concept discussion and an operating service visible in every exported copy.
